summary: A republication of PKCS #9 version 2.0 from RSA Laboratories, selecting object classes and attribute types for use in other PKCS standards. Change control remains within the PKCS process.

plainLanguage.summary: This republishes a company's list of standard labels used by its security specifications.

subtitle: A catalog of directory object classes and attribute types for PKCS-based public-key systems, republished by the IETF.

tldr.problem: Public-key standards such as PKCS #7, #10, #12 and #15 needed shared, well-defined attribute types and directory object classes for names, signatures, requests and stored keys.
tldr.mechanism: PKCS #9 v2.0 defines two auxiliary object classes, pkcsEntity and naturalPerson, plus attribute types and two matching rules, all written in ASN.1 with an LDAP-oriented BNF summary.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and republishes the RSA Laboratories specification, with change control kept inside the PKCS process.

today: RFC 2985 is an Informational memo from November 2000, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It is a republication of PKCS #9 v2.0, and change control stays within the PKCS process.

sections.title: What PKCS #9 Provides
sections.content:
This memo is a republication of PKCS #9 v2.0 from RSA Laboratories' Public-Key Cryptography Standards series. Everything except the security considerations section is taken directly from that specification, and change control stays within the PKCS process. It does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

It defines two new auxiliary object classes, pkcsEntity and naturalPerson, and selected attribute types for them. It also defines attribute types for PKCS #7 (and S/MIME CMS) signed messages, PKCS #10 certificate-signing requests, PKCS #12 personal information exchanges and PKCS #15 cryptographic tokens, with matching rules where needed. All definitions are in ASN.1, and Appendix B repeats most of them in BNF to ease use in LDAP environments.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a dictionary of agreed words for security paperwork, so every program spells the same thing the same way.

sections.title: The Two Object Classes
sections.content:
Both classes are auxiliary, meaning they add optional attributes to a directory entry, and both are meant for LDAP and X.500 directory services.

pkcsEntity holds attributes about PKCS-related entities: pKCS7PDU (a PKCS #7 ContentInfo), userPKCS12 (a PKCS #12 PFX), pKCS15Token (a software PKCS #15 token) and encryptedPrivateKeyInfo (a PKCS #8 encrypted private key).

naturalPerson holds attributes about human beings: emailAddress, unstructuredName, unstructuredAddress, dateOfBirth, placeOfBirth, gender, countryOfCitizenship, countryOfResidence, pseudonym and serialNumber. The country attributes SHALL be two-letter country codes. The gender value is a single letter, M or F in either case.
sections.plainLanguage: One sticker holds a person's security files, and another sticker holds facts about the person, like name and birthday.

sections.title: Attributes for Signed Messages
sections.content:
These attribute types go in the authenticated or unauthenticated attribute fields of a PKCS #7 SignerInfo (or a CMS AuthenticatedData value). contentType and messageDigest are required whenever any authenticated attributes are present. signingTime records when the signer purportedly signed; the RFC says correctness is not required and acceptance is the recipient's discretion.

randomNonce (at least four bytes) and sequenceNumber are alternatives for signers who cannot give a time, and help guard against replay attacks. A counterSignature is a signature over another signature and must be an unauthenticated attribute; it can itself carry a countersignature, so chains of any length are possible.

The time rules are quoted from CMS: dates from 1 January 1950 to 31 December 2049 are encoded as UTCTime and others as GeneralizedTime, in Zulu time with seconds included.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone signs a document, these labels say what it is, a fingerprint of it, when it was signed, and who double-checked the signature.

sections.title: Requests, Stored Keys and S/MIME Attributes
sections.content:
For PKCS #10 certification requests, challengePassword is a password by which an entity may request certificate revocation, and extensionRequest carries the certificate extensions the requester wants. The extendedCertificateAttributes attribute is deprecated because PKCS #6 became historic with X.509 v3.

For PKCS #12 and PKCS #15, friendlyName is a user-friendly name and localKeyId identifies a key locally within an application. For S/MIME, the memo mentions signingDescription and smimeCapabilities for completeness, since S/MIME defines them in the PKCS #9 identifier tree.

Two matching rules are defined: pkcs9CaseIgnoreMatch, which compares strings ignoring case (so "Pkcs" and "PKCS" match), and signingTimeMatch, which compares times.
sections.plainLanguage: There are extra labels for ordering a certificate, giving a stored key a nickname, and describing what a signed email is about.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Directory attributes describe real-world people, organizations and devices, and most countries have privacy laws about publishing information on people. The challengePassword attribute should not be stored unencrypted in a directory.

Attributes of the pkcsEntity class may be read by third parties, so they should be adequately protected. If a password-protected value (PKCS #8, #12 or #15) is stored, the directory should authenticate the requester before delivering it, to prevent an off-line password-search attack. The RFC notes that this raises non-repudiation issues, because the directory could itself try a password search.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these labels hold private facts, so the place where they are stored should check who is asking before handing them out.
